title: O Little Town of Bethlehem
description: Phillips Brooks's Christmas hymn in its UK version, to Henry Walford Davies's tune of 1905: the public-domain setting sung in Britain, not Vaughan Williams's "Forest Green". For 2 to 4 singers, gentle and unhurried: verses 1 and 3, and the refrain "O holy Child of Bethlehem" in Walford Davies's own four parts, the tune turning to A minor at "Yet in thy dark streets shineth".

credits.arrangement: Henry Walford Davies's refrain harmony (Worship Song, 1905), with parts for the verses on his organ chords, adapted by Stackapella

licence.words: public domain: Phillips Brooks died 23 January 1893 (Wikipedia, "Phillips Brooks"); sung as Worship Song (1905) prints them: its verses 1 and 3 ("O little town of Bethlehem" and "How silently, how silently"; its verse 2, "For Christ is born of Mary", is not sung) and its refrain, Brooks's last stanza "O holy Child of Bethlehem", the same stanzas our US version sings as verses 1, 3 and 4
licence.tune: public domain: Henry Walford Davies died 11 March 1941 (Wikipedia, "Walford Davies"; Hymnary.org gives 1869-1941); first printed, as far as we know, in Worship Song (1905), No. 661, headed "CHRISTMAS CAROL. [2nd tune.]" and "H. Walford Davies, Mus. Doc.", the page marked "Copyright, 1905, by W. Garrett Horder". This is not "Forest Green", the tune most UK churches sing to these words, whose harmony and adaptation are Vaughan Williams's and still in copyright in the UK
licence.arrangement: Worship Song (1905) prints the verses for sopranos over organ and only the refrain in four parts ("Refrain. Harmony."); notes are named here as written, a tone below the print. The refrain is Henry Walford Davies's own four parts (public domain: he died 1941), adapted for 2 to 4 beginners. In the verses the alto, tenor and bass are ours (Stackapella's), written on the chords of his organ part, which harmonizes the tune almost exactly as his refrain does, so they keep close to his refrain lines; there the alto sings D under the tune's F on "town" and "deep", adding a sixth to the organ's F chord so the duet has a third, not a unison, and the bass sits on G under "ev-er-last-ing", as the organ's pedal A (printed) does. The tune is Walford Davies's in its rhythm and notes, apart from breaths. Changes to his refrain parts: one note a syllable where a lower part moves within a syllable, the first of its notes ("we", "Cast", "and", "Be", "in" in "born in" for the bass, "the", "mas", "an-", "Oh,", "come", "a-", "man-"), except "ter" (alto E4 and tenor C4, his notes on its second half, so the tune's A4 does not sound over his B-flat 3), "out" (bass C3, his second note, so the alto's E is not doubled) and "bide" and "with" (alto E4, tenor G3, bass C3, the C chord his organ plays there in the verses: on the downbeat of "bide" his alto's F4 is a bare fifth under the tune's C5, and on its second half his A4 a bare fourth); "Lord" (one syllable over the tune's D5, C5, A4) is sung on one chord, F over A: alto F4, tenor F3, bass A2 (his chord moves B-flat, F over A, D minor over F, his bass B-flat 3, A3, F3). So that 2 and 3 singers have each chord's third and no unison, octave or bare fourth or fifth under the tune on a strong beat: the alto sings D4 on "Child" and "sin" (his F4, in unison with the tune), A3 on "in" ("enter in"), D4 on "Em-" and "Our" (F4 each time, in unison), E4 on "out" (his C4, then D4: a fourth under G4), D4 on "us" and "to-" (his E4: a fifth under B4; D is his tenor's seventh) and C4 on "day!" (E4: a fourth under A4 for three beats), C4 on "Christ-" (A3, an octave under A4), E4 on "gels" and "The" (C4, an octave under C5), and on "ti-dings" the alto and tenor exchange, the alto E4, D4 and the tenor A3, B3 (his alto A3, B3 and tenor E4, D4, which crosses above the alto and leaves the duet a seventh). For ranges and easy lines: the bass E3 on "us" (his E2, under a beginner bass; E3 is his next note); the tenor B3 on "to-" (his D4, a tritone from A-flat 3); the tenor A3 on "pray;" (his E3, a sixth below his C4 on "Cast"); the tenor G3 on "in" (his E3, F-sharp 3) and A3 on "day!" (C4); the bass on G2 through "great glad ti-dings" (his C3, E3, G3, G2), so it has no octave leap and no parallel octaves with the tune; the alto C4 on the first "O" (his F4), a third from the verse's last note, not a sixth. At the end, "Our Lord Em-man-u-el!": the tenor A3, F3, F3, E3, E3, F3 and the bass A2 on "Our" and "Lord" (his tenor C4, B-flat 3 to D4, A3, C4, B-flat 3, A3; his bass A3 and B-flat 3 to F3), the alto C4 on "man-" (his E4, a fourth under A4) and B-flat 3, A3 on "u-el!" (his E4, F4), so the last chord has root and third at every size (F4, A3, F3, F2; the tenor resolves its leading tone up rather than holding the bottom of its range) without crossings or parallel fifths; his bass divides on the last note (F2 and C3), sung F2. Breaths written in for beginners: the lines that end on a crotchet ("hem", "sleep", "neth", "years" and their places in each stanza) keep a quaver, the next pickup coming a semiquaver late; the held line ends ("lie", "by", "light") give up three quarters of a beat and "night" and "in" a whole beat before the next stanza. Not sung: the organ's introduction and interludes, verse 2, and the Amen. Accepted exceptions: the tune's C4 on the semiquaver pickups "The" ("The silent stars") and "Be", under the beginner soprano's D4, kept as the price of a key that puts every other part in range; E doubled in the A minor passages ("The silent stars", "Yet in thy dark streets", "We hear the Christmas angels") and at "The ev-er-", where E is the fifth of A minor or the third of C, not the leading tone (his tenor and bass sing E3 together at "We" and "the"). The alto sings F4 on "us," in "Oh, come to us, a-bide" (his C4), as our verse alto sings at "fears", which removes his alto and tenor's fifths there (they stood bare once his quavers were sung as one note a syllable). The alto's C4 on "hem!" sits a fourth under the tune on the line's last quaver (an A3 would leap into the next F4). In the verses the tenor sings C4 under "and dream-" and "to hu-" (the organ's D7), the notes of his refrain tenor at "and en-", and each stanza's last tenor note is F3.
licence.source: W. Garrett Horder (ed.), Worship Song, with Accompanying Tunes (London: Novello, 1905), No. 661, "Christmas Carol. [2nd tune.]", 8.6.8.6.7.6.8.6., "H. Walford Davies, Mus. Doc.", pp. 744-745, under "For the Young", signed "Phillips Brooks" and "Copyright, 1905, by W. Garrett Horder"; the verses for sopranos over organ, the refrain in four parts on two staves; in G major (one sharp), common time, with a crotchet pickup, as printed; written here in F, a tone lower, so his tenor's F-sharp 4 and bass's C4 and B3 sit in the beginner ranges; crotchet = 1. The book gives no tempo; 76 crotchets is gentle and unhurried. Read from the Trinity College, University of Toronto copy at archive.org/details/worshipsongwith00horduoft/page/n785 and n786. The words as printed there, with these differences from our US version's text (Hutchins, 1916): "Beth-le-hem," and "lie!" (US "Bethlehem!" and "lie;"), "sleep," with a comma, "light;" (US "Light;"), "to-night!" (US "to-night."); in verse 3 "com-ing;" (US "coming,") and "heaven." sung in one syllable (US "heav'n."); in the refrain "sin and" without a comma, "en-ter in" followed by a dash, left out here (US "enter in,"), "to-day!" (US "to-day.") and "Oh, come to us" (US "O come to us").
